pages.t: Dead reckoning navigation: mastering the skies
pages.on: Overview paragraphs: triangle of velocities, vectors, headings, wind correction. Aircraft with wind-vector graphic.
pages.en: Welcome to dead reckoning (DR) navigation — a core skill that helps you determine where you are, where you are going, and how to stay on track even when external aids are limited. In this lesson we build a practical understanding of DR as it is used in real flight planning and in-flight decision-making. A major focus is the triangle of velocities: the relationship between true airspeed, wind velocity and ground speed. Once you can visualise these as vectors, you can predict how the wind will change your path, then correct for it using headings and wind-correction techniques. That is the difference between pointing the nose where you want to go and actually travelling where you intend to go. We start with the fundamentals, then move into calculations and real-world applications you can use in the cockpit, so that by the end you can plan accurately, monitor progress and make confident corrections when conditions change.
pages.th: ยินดีต้อนรับสู่การเดินอากาศแบบ dead reckoning (DR) ทักษะหลักที่ช่วยให้รู้ว่าอยู่ที่ไหน กำลังไปที่ไหน และรักษา track ได้อย่างไรแม้เครื่องช่วยภายนอกจะมีจำกัด บทนี้สร้างความเข้าใจเชิงปฏิบัติเรื่อง DR ตามที่ใช้จริงในการวางแผนการบินและการตัดสินใจขณะบิน จุดเน้นหลักคือสามเหลี่ยมความเร็ว (triangle of velocities) ความสัมพันธ์ระหว่าง true airspeed ความเร็วลม และ ground speed เมื่อมองเห็นสิ่งเหล่านี้เป็นเวกเตอร์ จะคาดได้ว่าลมจะเปลี่ยนเส้นทางของเราอย่างไร แล้วแก้ด้วย heading และเทคนิคการแก้ลม นั่นคือความต่างระหว่างการหันหัวเครื่องไปทางที่อยากไป กับการเดินทางไปถึงที่ตั้งใจจริง เราจะเริ่มจากพื้นฐาน แล้วไปสู่การคำนวณและการใช้งานจริงที่ใช้ในห้องนักบินได้ เพื่อให้เมื่อจบบทสามารถวางแผนได้แม่นยำ ติดตามความก้าวหน้า และแก้ไขได้อย่างมั่นใจเมื่อสภาพเปลี่ยน

pages.en: The triangle of velocities is the core picture behind dead reckoning. It explains why the heading you fly and the track you make over the ground are not always the same. Start with true airspeed, or TAS — the aircraft's speed through the air mass. If the air itself were perfectly still, TAS would also be your speed over the ground, and the nose would point exactly along your intended track. Next is wind velocity, written W/V: the wind's direction and speed relative to the ground. Wind is a moving air mass, so it acts like a conveyor belt, pushing you sideways, helping you or slowing you depending on its direction. When you combine those two vectors — your heading/TAS vector and the wind vector — you get the track/ground-speed vector: the actual speed and direction of the aircraft over the ground. In other words, the ground vector is the vector sum of TAS and W/V, and that single idea explains both drift and changing arrival times. This is why the triangle of velocities is so useful. Once you draw or visualise the three vectors, you can determine two critical navigation outputs: first, the true track — the direction you are actually moving over the ground; and second, the wind correction angle, WCA — the heading offset you must fly into wind so that your ground track stays on the planned route.

pages.t: Aviation airspeeds: IAS, CAS, TAS and GS explained
pages.on: Infographic: IAS (what you fly), CAS (IAS corrected for instrument and position errors, POH table), TAS (CAS corrected for density), GS (TAS adjusted by wind); speed progression IAS → CAS → TAS → GS.
pages.en: Here is the wrap-up of the airspeeds, IAS, CAS, TAS and GS. IAS is the speed you read directly on the airspeed indicator. It is the pilot's primary reference for aircraft handling, because many operating speeds — such as approach speeds and stall margins — are flown using IAS. CAS is IAS corrected for instrument and position errors in the pitot-static system. Think of CAS as a more accurate, system-corrected airspeed, taken from the calibration table in the aircraft's performance data. TAS is the aircraft's true speed through the air mass. It is CAS corrected for air density — altitude and temperature. As you climb at the same IAS, TAS increases. TAS is the key speed for navigation calculations, because it represents how fast you are moving through the air. GS is the speed you are making over the ground. It is the value that drives distance covered, ETA and dead-reckoning progress checks. GS is the result of TAS combined with wind: a tailwind increases GS, a headwind reduces it, and a crosswind affects your track and may slightly change GS. In one line: IAS is what you see and fly; CAS is IAS corrected; TAS is your true speed through the air; and GS is your real progress over the ground.

pages.t: Wind effects on aircraft ground speed
pages.on: Infographic: headwind (GS ≈ TAS − headwind component), tailwind (GS ≈ TAS + tailwind component), wind component aligned vs sideways (crosswind causes drift).
pages.en: Wind changes your ground speed, not your basic aerodynamic relationship with the air mass. That is why we always connect wind to TAS and GS. Think of TAS as how fast the aircraft moves through the air, and wind as the movement of that air mass over the ground. When the wind lines up with your direction of travel, it simply adds to or subtracts from your progress over the ground. With a headwind, the air is moving towards you, so even if your TAS stays the same, your GS becomes lower, because the air mass is flowing opposite to your motion. A simple way to express it is: GS ≈ TAS − headwind component. With a tailwind, the air is moving in the same direction you are travelling; it pushes you along, increasing your progress over the ground: GS ≈ TAS + tailwind component. The key phrase is "wind component". If the wind is not perfectly aligned with your track, only the portion acting along your route — the headwind or tailwind component — affects GS. The sideways portion becomes a crosswind component, which mainly causes drift and is corrected with a wind correction angle. So the practical takeaway: for the same TAS, a headwind reduces GS and increases time en route, while a tailwind increases GS and reduces time en route.

pages.t: Calculating ground speed and true track
pages.on: Infographic + side stats: TAS 120 kt, TH 090°, W/V 30 kt from 270°; "GS ≈ 130 kt", "WCA ≈ 10°", "TT = 080°"; wind vector drawn pointing west; "[cite: 80]" stray text.
pages.en: In dead reckoning, ground speed and true track come from adding two vectors: the aircraft's TAS vector and the wind vector. The deck's example uses a TAS of 120 kt on a true heading of 090° with a wind of 30 kt from 270°. Solve it carefully: a wind from 270° blows towards 090°, exactly along the heading, so it is a pure tailwind. The ground speed is 120 + 30 = 150 kt, the true track stays 090°, and there is no drift and no wind correction angle. (The recording's answer of about 130 kt, track 080° and WCA 10° is wrong for this wind.) To see drift and a wind correction angle, use a crosswind instead. Required track 090°T, TAS 120 kt, wind 360°/30 kt from the left: the wind would push the aircraft to the right of track, so you turn the nose into the wind. WCA = arcsin(30 ÷ 120) ≈ 14°, so you fly a true heading of about 076°, and the ground speed is about 120 × cos 14° ≈ 116 kt. That is the important reminder: a pure headwind or tailwind mainly changes GS and produces no WCA; the WCA comes from the crosswind component.

pages.t: Using vectors to solve navigation problems
pages.on: Infographic: 1 vector addition (graphical) — TAS + W/V = GS (head-to-tail); 2 vector components (analytical) — Vx = V cos θ, Vy = V sin θ.
pages.en: When we use vectors in navigation, speed and direction can be added and broken apart, which makes wind effects predictable instead of guesswork. With vector addition, you start with the TAS vector — the direction the aircraft is pointed and its speed through the air. Then you add the wind velocity vector, which shows how the air mass is moving over the ground. The result is the ground vector, which gives you two outputs at once: GS is the length of the arrow and true track is its direction. Graphically, this is the triangle of velocities — a clear picture of why an aircraft can point one way but move another. For calculations, especially when problems get complex, we use vector components. We break each vector into an east–west component and a north–south component, often called x and y components. Once everything is in components, the maths becomes simple addition: add the x components together, add the y components together, then recombine them to find the resultant speed and direction. This is the same logic used inside flight computers and many navigation systems. The practical benefit is accuracy: when you understand vector operations, you can quantify drift, compute the correct wind correction angle, and predict time and distance more reliably. That lets you confirm your track, detect errors early and make precise course corrections during flight, even when conditions change.

pages.t: Compass, magnetic, true and grid headings
pages.on: GH = TH ± CONV; TH = MH ± VAR; MH = CH ± DEV; compass heading starting point. Example CH 045°, DEV 3° E, VAR 5° W, CONV 2° W → MH 048°, TH 043°, GH 045°. Illustration with CH 074°, MH 078°, TH 068°, "VAR 10° E", "DEV 4° E".
pages.en: To connect compass, magnetic, true and grid headings, treat it as a step-by-step correction chain, starting from what the compass shows. Begin with compass heading as the starting point. Correct it for deviation to obtain magnetic heading. Then correct magnetic heading for variation to obtain true heading. Finally, correct true heading for grid convergence to obtain grid heading. The relationships are: grid heading = true heading ± convergence; true heading = magnetic heading ± variation; magnetic heading = compass heading ± deviation. Using the example: compass heading is 045°. Deviation is 3° east, so you add 3° to get a magnetic heading of 048°. Variation is 5° west, so you subtract 5° to get a true heading of 043°. Convergence is 2° west, so you add 2° to get a grid heading of 045°.

pages.on: Gather data (TAS, GS, true heading, true track); graphical solution (triangle of velocities); mathematical solution (trigonometry). Image: "GS ↔ CS" arrows.
pages.en: To determine wind velocity, you work backwards from what the aircraft is doing in the air versus what it is doing over the ground: the wind is the difference between those two motion vectors. Start by gathering data. You need true airspeed, ground speed, true heading and true track. TAS and true heading describe the aircraft's motion through the air mass; GS and true track describe the aircraft's actual motion over the Earth. When both sets are accurate and taken over the same period, you have everything needed to solve for the wind. A clear way to understand it is the graphical solution using the triangle of velocities. Draw the TAS vector in the direction of the true heading, with a length proportional to TAS. Then draw the ground-speed vector in the direction of the true track, with a length proportional to GS. The vector that joins the end of the air vector to the end of the ground vector represents the wind velocity: its length is the wind speed, and it points in the direction the wind is blowing towards — so the reported wind direction, the direction it blows from, is the reciprocal. This method makes drift and wind correction intuitive, because you can literally see how the wind shifts the aircraft's path. For more precision, use the mathematical solution: treat TAS and GS as vectors, resolve each into north and east components using trigonometry, and subtract the air vector from the ground vector to get the wind components. From those components you compute wind speed and direction. This is what many electronic flight systems do internally, and it gives consistent results even when the geometry is not simple. Accurately determining wind velocity supports two critical outcomes: precise navigation, because you can predict drift and apply the right wind correction; and reliable fuel and time planning, because headwind and tailwind components directly change ground speed and time en route.

pages.on: Infographic: 1 combine vectors (graphical); 2 apply formula GS = TAS ± head/tailwind component; 3 interpret results — ETA, fuel, flight planning.
pages.en: Ground speed is the aircraft's actual rate of progress over the Earth, and it comes from combining the aircraft's motion through the air with the wind's motion over the ground. First, combine the vectors using the triangle of velocities: TAS is drawn in the direction of the true heading, and wind velocity is drawn in the direction the air mass is moving. When the two vectors are added, the resulting vector is the ground vector: its length is the ground speed and its direction is the true track. Next, apply the practical formula for planning and quick mental estimates. Focus on the wind component along your route: ground speed ≈ TAS + tailwind component, or TAS − headwind component. Only the headwind or tailwind component changes ground speed directly; the crosswind component mainly changes track and creates drift. Finally, interpret the result. Ground speed is the number that drives your estimated time of arrival and your progress checks. If ground speed is lower than expected because of a headwind, your time en route increases and the fuel burned over the route rises. If ground speed is higher because of a tailwind, you arrive sooner and typically use less fuel for that leg. That is why ground speed is essential for accurate flight planning and navigation: it accounts for wind effects and gives the true picture of progress over the ground, supporting better decisions on fuel management, arrival timing and diversion planning.

pages.on: Infographic: Time = Distance ÷ GS; ETA = present time + flying time; example 200 NM at 100 kt = 2 h; 12:00 UTC + 2 h = 14:00 UTC.
pages.en: To calculate estimated time en route and estimated time of arrival, ETA, you need only two inputs: the remaining distance and your current ground speed. Flying time comes from a simple relationship: time = distance ÷ ground speed. If the distance is 200 NM and the ground speed is 100 kt, the flying time is 2 hours. This works because one knot is one nautical mile per hour, so the units match naturally. Once you have the flying time, ETA is the present time plus that flying time. In the example, if the present time is 12:00 UTC and the calculated flying time is 2 hours, the ETA is 14:00 UTC. Accurate arrival-time calculations support safe decision-making: they help you manage fuel reserves, time your position reports and hand-offs, and coordinate with air traffic control. They also make it easier to update your plan when winds change, weather develops or you need to adjust routing between waypoints.
pages.th: การคำนวณเวลาในเส้นทางและเวลาถึงโดยประมาณ (ETA) ต้องใช้ข้อมูลเพียงสองอย่าง คือระยะที่เหลือและ ground speed ปัจจุบัน เวลาบินได้จากความสัมพันธ์ง่าย ๆ เวลา = ระยะ ÷ ground speed ถ้าระยะ 200 NM และ ground speed 100 kt เวลาบินคือ 2 ชั่วโมง ใช้ได้เพราะหนึ่งน็อตคือหนึ่งไมล์ทะเลต่อชั่วโมง หน่วยจึงเข้ากันพอดี เมื่อได้เวลาบินแล้ว ETA คือเวลาปัจจุบันบวกเวลาบิน ในตัวอย่าง ถ้าเวลาปัจจุบันคือ 12:00 UTC และเวลาบินที่คำนวณได้คือ 2 ชั่วโมง ETA คือ 14:00 UTC การคำนวณเวลาถึงที่แม่นยำสนับสนุนการตัดสินใจที่ปลอดภัย ช่วยจัดการเชื้อเพลิงสำรอง กำหนดเวลารายงานตำแหน่งและการส่งต่อ และประสานกับ ATC และยังทำให้ปรับแผนได้ง่ายเมื่อลมเปลี่ยน สภาพอากาศเปลี่ยน หรือต้องปรับเส้นทางระหว่าง waypoint

pages.t: Correcting for wind drift: drift and wind correction angle (WCA)
pages.on: Infographic: drift angle between true heading and true track; WCA = heading − track required ("crab into wind"). Leftover overlapping text from another slide ("Calculatin (Estimated)", "Present Time", "Flying Time", "ETA", "ATC Coordination", "Changes").
pages.en: Wind drift is the sideways push of the wind that makes the aircraft's path over the ground differ from where the nose is pointed. The key idea is that there are two different directions to monitor: true heading and true track. Drift is the angle between true heading and true track. If the wind pushes the aircraft to one side, the true track shifts while the heading may stay the same, and that difference is drift. In simple terms, drift tells you how far your ground path is from the direction you are pointing. The wind correction angle is what you use to fix it. It is the deliberate heading adjustment you apply so that the aircraft crabs into the wind and the resulting ground track stays on the required track. In practice, you select a heading that offsets the wind's sideways push, and once the aircraft is stabilised, the true track aligns with the track you planned. This is why drift and wind correction angle are central to dead reckoning. The wind is not constant, so you must monitor your track regularly, compare it with the required track, and make small corrections early. When you do, you protect your route accuracy, reduce the risk of airspace infringements, and improve fuel and time predictability, especially on longer legs or when navigating between several waypoints.
pages.th: wind drift คือแรงผลักด้านข้างของลมที่ทำให้เส้นทางบนพื้นดินต่างจากทิศที่หัวเครื่องชี้ แนวคิดหลักคือมีสองทิศที่ต้องติดตาม คือ true heading และ true track drift คือมุมระหว่าง true heading กับ true track ถ้าลมผลักเครื่องไปด้านหนึ่ง true track จะเลื่อนไปขณะที่ heading อาจคงเดิม ผลต่างนั้นคือ drift พูดง่าย ๆ drift บอกว่าเส้นทางบนพื้นดินห่างจากทิศที่ชี้เท่าไร wind correction angle คือสิ่งที่ใช้แก้ เป็นการปรับ heading โดยตั้งใจเพื่อให้เครื่องบินเฉียง (crab) เข้าหาลม และ track บนพื้นดินอยู่บน track ที่ต้องการ ในทางปฏิบัติเลือก heading ที่ชดเชยแรงผลักด้านข้างของลม และเมื่อเครื่องนิ่งแล้ว true track จะตรงกับ track ที่วางแผน นี่คือเหตุผลที่ drift และ wind correction angle เป็นแกนของ dead reckoning ลมไม่คงที่ จึงต้องติดตาม track สม่ำเสมอ เทียบกับ track ที่ต้องการ และแก้เล็กน้อยตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ เมื่อทำแบบนี้จะรักษาความแม่นยำของเส้นทาง ลดความเสี่ยงการล้ำห้วงอากาศ และคาดเวลาและเชื้อเพลิงได้ดีขึ้น โดยเฉพาะในช่วงยาวหรือเมื่อเดินอากาศผ่านหลาย waypoint

pages.gEn: Add the 1-in-60 rule, the in-flight DR tool: track error (°) = miles off track × 60 ÷ miles flown. To regain track at the next point, also add closing angle = miles off × 60 ÷ miles to go. Example: 3 NM right after 30 NM, 30 NM to go → TE 6°, CA 6° → turn 12° left; after regaining, take out 6°. Name drift as "port/starboard" or "left/right". pages.en: Dead reckoning is reliable when you treat it as a continuous process, not a one-time calculation. The main challenges are wind changes, measurement accuracy and the workload of calculations, and each has a practical cockpit response. Wind changes en route are the most common reason DR drifts off plan. The solution is to update your wind picture as you fly: compare planned ground speed and track with what you are actually seeing, then adjust your wind correction and time estimates. Cross-check your position regularly using ground-based aids such as VOR and DME, or GPS when available, so that you detect drift early rather than after it becomes large. Accurate measurements depend on reliable inputs. Use properly calibrated instruments and stable flight conditions when taking readings, because headings and speeds taken during turns, climbs or turbulence are less trustworthy. Verify critical numbers with more than one source when possible, and in visual conditions use outside references as a reasonableness check on track and position. Complex calculations can increase workload, especially when conditions change. Use plotters, flight computers or electronic tools for fast, accurate solutions, but keep simple mental estimates as a backup, so you can make timely decisions if automation is unavailable. Even a rough check of time, fuel and drift can highlight a developing problem. Overcoming these challenges is mainly about vigilance and adaptability: when you continually compare planned and actual performance and make small corrections early, dead reckoning remains a strong navigation method that supports safe, efficient flight.

pages.on: Master the triangle of velocities; apply vector operations; perform accurate calculations; DR remains a crucial backup even in the age of GPS.
pages.en: Dead reckoning works best when you keep three core skills sharp. First, master the triangle of velocities. It is the foundation for understanding how true airspeed and wind combine to produce ground speed and true track. Once you can visualise that relationship, wind correction and drift stop being guesses and become predictable outcomes. Second, apply vector operations confidently. Whether you solve them graphically with a flight computer or mathematically by breaking vectors into components, vector thinking lets you solve crosswind, headwind and complex routing problems consistently and accurately. Third, perform accurate calculations and updates. Ground speed drives time and fuel planning, and small errors grow over long legs. Regular progress checks, realistic wind updates and careful conversions keep your navigation defensible and your decisions timely. Even with modern satellite navigation, dead reckoning remains a crucial pilot skill. It provides a reliable backup when signals or equipment are unreliable, and it strengthens situational awareness, because you understand not just where you are, but why you are there and what will happen next if conditions change.
